claims.text: Adding a low concentration of a minor alloying element to a phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy improves its glass-forming ability.
Adding a low concentration of a minor alloying element to such an alloy improves the thermal stability of its amorphous state.
The proposed addition is a micro-alloying element distinct from the primary alloy constituents.
The intervention is effective only within a defined low-concentration window.
The added element enhances local atomic packing.
Enhanced local atomic packing reduces the density of crystallization nucleation sites.
The added element interacts with phosphorus.
Interaction between the added element and phosphorus modifies local chemical bonding.
Interaction between the added element and phosphorus modifies local atomic arrangements.
The modified bonding and atomic arrangements reduce the free-energy driving force for crystallization.
Reducing the free-energy driving force for crystallization stabilizes the amorphous phase.
The modified alloy will have a lower critical cooling rate for glass formation than the otherwise comparable alloy without the addition.
The modified alloy will have a higher crystallization onset temperature than the otherwise comparable alloy without the addition.
Excessive addition of the micro-alloying element may cause phase separation.
Excessive addition may open alternative crystallization pathways.
Phase separation or alternative crystallization pathways can negate the beneficial effects of the addition.

contradictions.description: The prediction jointly asserts both a lower critical cooling rate and a higher crystallization onset temperature, but the falsification rule requires failure to improve either metric. Thus, improvement in only one metric would avoid falsification despite failing the full predicted outcome.
